title: Enzyme kinetics and mechanisms
outcomes: Effects of pH and temperature on enzyme activity

summary.overview: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy (ΔG‡); they never change the equilibrium. Kinetics describes how fast an enzyme works (Vmax, kcat), how well it binds its substrate (Km), and how inhibitors change these values.

sections.heading: How enzymes catalyse
points: Enzymes lower ΔG‡ only. ΔG°′ and K′eq are unchanged, so equilibrium is simply reached faster.
Binding energy holds reactants close together and correctly oriented, and the active site binds the transition state more tightly than the substrate.
Acid–base catalysis: residues such as His, Asp and Glu donate or remove protons.
Covalent catalysis: a transient enzyme–substrate bond, e.g. the Schiff base in Class I aldolase.
Metal-ion catalysis: orienting the substrate, redox, and shielding charge, e.g. Mg²⁺–ATP in kinases.

sections.heading: Michaelis–Menten kinetics
points: v0 = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Measure initial rates, while [P] ≈ 0.
Km = [S] at which v0 = ½Vmax. As a rough guide, a lower Km means tighter binding.
kcat is the turnover number; Vmax = kcat[E]t.
kcat/Km measures catalytic efficiency; its diffusion limit is ≈ 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹.
Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v0 vs 1/[S]): y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = −1/Km, slope = Km/Vmax.

sections.heading: Inhibition
points: Competitive: binds the active site of free E. Km rises, Vmax is unchanged, and the lines meet on the y-axis. High [S] overcomes it.
Uncompetitive: binds ES only. Km and Vmax both fall, and the lines are parallel.
Mixed: binds both E and ES. Vmax falls, Km changes, and the lines meet left of the y-axis. Non-competitive is the special case where Km is unchanged.
Irreversible: covalent inactivation (e.g. organophosphates on acetylcholinesterase) removes active enzyme, so Vmax falls.

sections.heading: Two substrates, pH and temperature
points: Sequential mechanisms (a ternary complex forms) give intersecting lines; ping-pong mechanisms give parallel lines.
The pH optimum reflects the ionisation state of catalytic and binding groups; extremes of pH denature the enzyme.
The rate rises with temperature until the protein denatures.

keyTerms.definition: Energy barrier to reach the transition state; enzymes lower it.
Substrate concentration giving half of Vmax.
Maximum rate when the enzyme is saturated; Vmax = kcat[E]t.
Turnover number: substrate molecules converted per active site per second.
Specificity constant, a measure of catalytic efficiency.
Competes with the substrate for the active site; raises apparent Km.
Binds the ES complex only; lowers both Km and Vmax.
First product leaves before the second substrate binds.

examTips: Km is not the same as Kd: they are equal only when k2 ≪ k−1.
Read Vmax changes from the y-intercept and Km changes from the x-intercept. Competitive inhibition leaves 1/Vmax unchanged.
Parallel Lineweaver–Burk lines mean uncompetitive inhibition OR a ping-pong mechanism; check what was varied.
Enzymes never make an unfavourable reaction favourable; they only reach equilibrium faster.

questions.stem: Which definition of Km is always true for an enzyme that follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics?

options.text: The substrate concentration at which v0 = ½ Vmax
options.why: Setting [S] = Km in v0 = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) gives v0 = Vmax/2, whatever the mechanism.

options.text: The dissociation constant of the ES complex
options.why: Km equals Kd only when k2 ≪ k−1; in general Km = (k−1 + k2)/k1.

options.text: The maximum rate reached when the enzyme is saturated
options.why: That is Vmax.

options.text: The number of substrate molecules converted per enzyme per second
options.why: That is kcat, the turnover number.

questions.stem: An enzyme obeys Michaelis–Menten kinetics. At [S] = 4 Km, what is v0 as a fraction of Vmax?

options.why: This inverts the ratio; 0.25 would be v0/Vmax at [S] = Km/3.
Half of Vmax is reached at [S] = Km, not 4 Km.
Vmax is only approached asymptotically; it is never reached at a finite [S].

questions.stem: Which quantity does an enzyme change for the reaction it catalyses?

options.text: The activation free energy, ΔG‡
options.why: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering ΔG‡, mainly by binding the transition state more tightly than the substrate.

options.text: The standard free-energy change, ΔG°′
options.why: ΔG°′ depends only on the initial and final states, which the enzyme does not change.

options.text: The equilibrium constant, K′eq
options.why: K′eq is fixed by ΔG°′; an enzyme speeds up both directions equally.

options.text: The final ratio of product to substrate at equilibrium
options.why: This is K′eq again; enzymes only reach equilibrium faster.

questions.stem: Two substrates compete for the same enzyme. Which parameter best predicts which substrate will be converted faster when both are at low concentration?

options.text: kcat/Km (the specificity constant)
options.why: At [S] ≪ Km, v0 ≈ (kcat/Km)[E]t[S], so kcat/Km sets the relative rates; its upper limit is diffusion (10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹).

options.text: kcat alone (the turnover number)
options.why: kcat describes the saturated enzyme; at low [S], binding (Km) matters as much as turnover.

options.text: Km alone (the substrate affinity)
options.why: A low Km means good binding, but a slow kcat could still make conversion slow.

options.text: Vmax (the maximum velocity)
options.why: Vmax depends on enzyme concentration and describes saturating, not low, [S].

questions.stem: A Lineweaver–Burk plot cuts the x-axis at −0.5 mM⁻¹ and the y-axis at 0.02 min/µmol. What are Km and Vmax?

options.text: Km = 2 mM; Vmax = 50 µmol/min
options.why: x-intercept = −1/Km, so Km = 2 mM; y-intercept = 1/Vmax, so Vmax = 50 µmol/min.

options.text: Km = 0.5 mM; Vmax = 0.02 µmol/min
options.why: The intercepts are reciprocals and must be inverted.

options.text: Km = 50 mM; Vmax = 2 µmol/min
options.why: This swaps the two intercepts: the x-axis gives Km and the y-axis gives Vmax.

options.text: Km = −2 mM; Vmax = 50 µmol/min
options.why: The x-intercept is −1/Km; Km itself is positive.

questions.stem: Lineweaver–Burk lines measured with and without an inhibitor meet on the y-axis. What type of inhibition is this?

options.text: Competitive: apparent Km increases, Vmax unchanged
options.why: Same y-intercept (1/Vmax) but a steeper slope (αKm/Vmax): high [S] can outcompete the inhibitor.

options.text: Uncompetitive: apparent Km and Vmax both decrease
options.why: Uncompetitive inhibition gives parallel lines.

options.text: Mixed: the lines meet to the left of the y-axis
options.why: Mixed inhibition changes Vmax, so the y-intercept moves.

options.text: Irreversible: Vmax decreases while Km is unchanged
options.why: Lowering Vmax would raise the y-intercept; here the y-intercept is unchanged.

questions.stem: An inhibitor binds only to the ES complex. Which kinetic pattern results?

options.text: Apparent Vmax and Km both fall by the same factor; Lineweaver–Burk lines are parallel
options.why: Uncompetitive: Vmax/α′ and Km/α′, so the slope Km/Vmax stays the same and the lines are parallel.

options.text: Apparent Km rises while Vmax is unchanged; the lines meet on the y-axis
options.why: That is competitive inhibition, where the inhibitor binds free E.

options.text: Vmax falls while Km is unchanged; the Lineweaver–Burk lines meet on the x-axis
options.why: That is pure non-competitive inhibition (a special case of mixed), where the inhibitor binds E and ES equally.

options.text: No change, because the substrate is already bound when the inhibitor arrives
options.why: Binding to ES blocks catalysis, so it does inhibit.

questions.stem: A dog has drunk antifreeze (ethylene glycol). Fomepizole is given: it binds the active site of alcohol dehydrogenase, which would otherwise convert ethylene glycol into toxic metabolites. What is its effect on ADH kinetics for ethylene glycol?

options.text: Apparent Km increases; Vmax unchanged
options.why: Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor. By raising the apparent Km, it slows ethylene glycol oxidation at the substrate concentrations found in the body.

options.text: Vmax decreases; Km unchanged
options.why: That pattern fits pure non-competitive or irreversible inhibition, not an active-site competitor.

options.text: Km and Vmax both decrease
options.why: That is uncompetitive inhibition, which needs the inhibitor to bind the ES complex.

options.text: kcat increases, so ethylene glycol is cleared faster
options.why: Inhibitors do not increase kcat; the aim is to slow formation of toxic metabolites.

questions.stem: Organophosphate insecticides covalently modify the active-site serine of acetylcholinesterase in poisoned livestock. Measured on the remaining active enzyme, what kinetic change does this produce?

options.text: Vmax decreases while Km is unchanged, and adding more substrate cannot reverse it
options.why: Irreversible inactivation removes enzyme molecules, lowering [E]t and so Vmax; the surviving enzyme still has its normal Km.

options.text: Km increases while Vmax is unchanged, and excess acetylcholine restores activity
options.why: That describes reversible competitive inhibition; a covalent adduct does not dissociate.

options.text: Km and Vmax both decrease, with parallel Lineweaver–Burk lines
options.why: That is uncompetitive inhibition, which needs reversible binding to ES.

options.text: No change in kinetics; only the enzyme's half-life changes
options.why: Losing active enzyme directly reduces the maximum rate.

questions.stem: Which statement about mixed inhibition is correct?

options.text: It binds both E and ES, Vmax decreases, and Lineweaver–Burk lines meet left of the y-axis
options.why: Mixed inhibitors bind a site away from the active site, on both E and ES; non-competitive is the special case where Km is unchanged.

options.text: The inhibitor binds only the active site of free enzyme, and the lines meet on the y-axis
options.why: That describes competitive inhibition.

options.text: The inhibitor binds only the ES complex, and the Lineweaver–Burk lines run parallel
options.why: That describes uncompetitive inhibition.

options.text: Vmax is unchanged because high [S] displaces the inhibitor
options.why: Mixed inhibitors also bind ES, so substrate cannot fully overcome them and Vmax falls.

questions.stem: Why are transition-state analogues often far more potent inhibitors than substrate analogues?

options.text: Active sites are complementary to the transition state, so they bind its mimics more tightly than substrate
options.why: Pauling's idea: extra interactions with the transition state lower ΔG‡, and analogues capture that extra binding energy.

options.text: Transition-state analogues bind covalently to the enzyme, so they are not released from the active site
options.why: Most are reversible, non-covalent inhibitors; their potency comes from complementarity.

options.text: They bind an allosteric site distinct from the active site, which locks the enzyme in its inactive T state
options.why: They bind the active site, because they mimic the transition state formed there.

options.text: They increase ΔG′° of the reaction, making it thermodynamically unfavourable for the enzyme to catalyse
options.why: Inhibitors do not change the thermodynamics of the reaction.

questions.stem: Histidine is a common general acid–base catalyst in active sites. What property makes it especially suitable?

options.text: Its imidazole pKa (≈ 6) is close to physiological pH, so it can donate or accept protons
options.why: Near pH 7, significant fractions are protonated and unprotonated, so His can shuttle protons in both directions.

options.text: It is the only amino acid with an ionisable side chain, so it is the only one that can move protons
options.why: Asp, Glu, Lys, Arg, Cys and Tyr also have ionisable side chains used in catalysis.

options.text: Its side chain is permanently positively charged at all pH values
options.why: A permanently charged group cannot both donate and accept protons; that describes Arg more closely.

options.text: It forms transient disulfide bonds with the substrate that hold it in place during catalysis
options.why: Disulfides involve Cys, and they are not part of acid–base catalysis.

questions.stem: Class I aldolase forms a Schiff base between an active-site lysine and its substrate. Which catalytic strategy is this?

options.text: Covalent catalysis
options.why: A transient covalent enzyme–substrate bond (Lys ε-amino group to the carbonyl) changes the reaction pathway.

options.text: Metal-ion catalysis
options.why: Class I aldolase uses no metal; zinc-dependent Class II aldolases are found mainly in microbes.

options.text: Proximity effects only
options.why: Proximity helps, but forming a covalent intermediate is the defining feature here.

options.text: Allosteric activation
options.why: Allostery involves effector binding at a separate site, not a covalent link to the substrate.

questions.stem: Kinases use Mg²⁺–ATP rather than free ATP as their substrate. What is the main catalytic role of the Mg²⁺?

options.text: It shields the negative charges of the phosphates and orients ATP for nucleophilic attack
options.why: Metal ions bind substrates in a set orientation and stabilise developing negative charge; they act electrostatically.

options.text: It is reduced to Mg⁺ and drives the phosphoryl transfer
options.why: Mg²⁺ is not redox active in biology; redox roles belong to transition metals such as Fe and Cu.

options.text: It forms a covalent bond with the γ-phosphate that is transferred to the enzyme
options.why: Mg²⁺ coordinates the phosphates; it is not covalently transferred.

options.text: It is a tightly bound prosthetic group, making the kinase a metalloenzyme
options.why: Mg²⁺ binds loosely from solution, so kinases are metal-activated enzymes rather than metalloenzymes.

questions.outcome: Effects of pH and temperature on enzyme activity
questions.stem: Why do many enzymes show a bell-shaped pH–activity curve with a clear optimum?

options.text: Catalytic and binding groups must be in the right ionisation state, and extreme pH denatures the protein
options.why: Moving away from the optimum protonates or deprotonates key residues (and the substrate); at extremes, folding is lost.

options.text: pH changes ΔG°′ of the reaction, and the optimum is where ΔG°′ is most negative
options.why: The pH optimum reflects the enzyme's ionisation state, not reaction thermodynamics.

options.text: H⁺ ions are a cofactor needed by most enzymes, so activity peaks where the H⁺ supply is just right
options.why: H⁺ is not a general cofactor; the effect works through ionisable groups.

options.text: Enzymes are soluble only at their pH optimum, so at other pH values they precipitate out of solution
options.why: Solubility is not what limits activity across the physiological pH range.

questions.outcome: Effects of pH and temperature on enzyme activity
questions.stem: A serum enzyme assay validated at 37 °C is accidentally run at 60 °C, and the measured activity is much lower. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The enzyme is denatured by heat, and loss of its native fold outweighs the faster rate expected
options.why: Activity rises with temperature until the protein unfolds; above that point, inactivation dominates.

options.text: Higher temperature lowers reaction rates, because the molecules move too fast to bind
options.why: Below the denaturation point, rates increase with temperature.

options.text: Km decreases at high temperature, so the enzyme becomes saturated and slows to a minimum
options.why: Saturation would raise v0 towards Vmax, not lower it.

options.text: Heat converts the active enzyme back into its inactive zymogen by re-joining the cleaved peptide
options.why: Zymogen activation is an irreversible proteolytic cleavage; heat cannot reverse it.

questions.stem: Why are kinetic measurements made on the initial velocity v0?

options.text: [S] is known and barely changed, and too little product has formed for reverse reaction or inhibition
options.why: The derivation assumes [P] ≈ 0 and a steady state of ES, which holds only early in the reaction.

options.text: The enzyme is not yet fully folded at later times, so only early rates reflect its true activity
options.why: The enzyme is folded and active throughout the assay.

options.text: v0 is equal to Vmax, so it gives the enzyme's maximum rate directly from a single measurement
options.why: v0 depends on [S]; it approaches Vmax only at saturating [S].

options.text: Km changes as the reaction proceeds, so it can only be measured before the substrate starts to run out
options.why: Km is a constant; the measured rate drifts because [S] falls and [P] rises.

questions.stem: For a two-substrate enzyme, 1/v0 versus 1/[A] is plotted at several fixed [B], giving a set of parallel lines. What does this indicate?

options.text: A ping-pong (double-displacement) mechanism
options.why: The first product leaves before the second substrate binds, so changing [B] gives parallel lines.

options.text: An ordered sequential (ternary-complex) mechanism
options.why: Sequential mechanisms form a ternary complex and give lines that intersect.

options.text: A random sequential (ternary-complex) mechanism
options.why: Random sequential is also a ternary-complex mechanism with intersecting lines.

options.text: Competitive inhibition of substrate A by substrate B
options.why: That would give lines meeting on the y-axis, not parallel lines.

flashcards.back: Turnover number: substrate molecules converted per active site per second at saturation. Vmax = kcat[E]t.
Specificity constant (catalytic efficiency). Limited by diffusion to ≈ 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ (e.g. acetylcholinesterase, fumarase).

flashcards.front: Competitive inhibition: Km, Vmax, LB plot?
flashcards.back: Apparent Km increases (αKm), Vmax unchanged, lines meet on the y-axis.

flashcards.front: Uncompetitive inhibition: Km, Vmax, LB plot?
flashcards.back: Binds ES only. Km and Vmax both fall by α′, slope Km/Vmax unchanged, lines parallel.

flashcards.front: Mixed inhibition: Km, Vmax, LB plot?
flashcards.back: Binds E and ES. Vmax falls, Km changes, lines meet left of the y-axis. Non-competitive = special case with Km unchanged.

flashcards.front: Irreversible inhibitor: kinetic effect? Veterinary example?
flashcards.back: Removes active enzyme, so Vmax falls and Km is unchanged; it cannot be overcome by substrate. Example: organophosphates acting on acetylcholinesterase.
Acid–base (proton donation and abstraction), covalent (transient enzyme–substrate bond), metal ion (orientation, redox, charge shielding).

flashcards.front: Do enzymes change ΔG°′ or K′eq?
flashcards.back: No. They lower ΔG‡ only, reaching the same equilibrium faster.
Metalloenzyme: tightly bound, usually a transition metal (Fe²⁺, Zn²⁺). Metal-activated: loosely binds Na⁺, K⁺ or Mg²⁺ from solution.

flashcards.outcome: Effects of pH and temperature on enzyme activity
flashcards.front: Why do enzymes have pH and temperature optima?
flashcards.back: pH: ionisation of catalytic and binding groups, with denaturation at extremes. Temperature: the rate rises until heat denatures the protein.
